description: ECDH-ES with HKDF [RFC 9053, Section 6.3]: a content key reaching a party whose public key is all the sender knows, either as the derived key itself (ECDH-ES + HKDF-256, -512) or wrapped by it (ECDH-ES + A128KW, A192KW, A256KW). These cases run through the cose-encrypt machinery — each produced by both implementations, compared, and handed to the other to open — and add what FINDINGS §12 asked of any ECDH-ES here: third-party values no agreement can supply — published by the COSE working group where an example exists, computed by the generator where none does, and labelled accordingly — a shared secret that begins with a zero byte on purpose, and points that must be refused rather than merely disagreed about. The ephemeral key is given rather than drawn, the second departure from default settings after deterministic signing and for the same reason: the bytes would otherwise be incomparable. Generated by tools/EcdhCases, which depends on neither implementation. Note what a passing case does NOT establish: an encrypted message says nothing about who sent it, and ECDH-ES in particular authenticates nobody — the static-static variants that would tell the recipient who sent it are implemented on neither side. Every key is printed in this file and secures nothing.

cases.description: ECDH-ES + HKDF-256 on P-256, from the COSE working group's example p256-hkdf-256-01: the content key is agreed with the recipient's public key rather than shared beforehand, and IS the derived key, so the message may have only this one recipient. The published secret, COSE_KDF_Context, content key and message are all checked — values that no agreement between the two implementations can supply, which is the condition FINDINGS §12 set. Its context is the one RFC 9052 Appendix C.3.1 prints: AlgorithmID is the content algorithm (A128GCM), never the ECDH algorithm.

The same on X25519 [RFC 7748], from the working group's example x25519-hkdf-256-direct. An X25519 key is one u-coordinate of 32 bytes, as an Ed25519 key is 32 bytes, and reading one as the other is what this case catches first.

ECDH-ES + A256KW on P-521 delivering an HMAC 512/512 key to a COSE_Mac, from the working group's example p521-wrap-256-03: the agreed key wraps the content key rather than being it, so AlgorithmID is A256KW. Two details of that example are reproduced on purpose: its generator kept the low 521 bits of the 66 random bytes it drew for the ephemeral key, and it sends a key identifier other than the recipient key's own.

A key pair found by searching: the shared x-coordinate on P-256 begins with a zero byte. The secret is that coordinate through I2OSP, left-padded to 32 bytes; an implementation taking it from a big-integer library that strips leading zeros derives a different key here and only here — about one message in 256 — which a set of fixed vectors would pass 255 times out of 256.

The same trap on P-521, where it is not rare at all: the top byte of the 66-byte coordinate carries a single bit, so roughly every second secret begins with a zero byte. An implementation that strips it fails half its P-521 messages, here through key wrap.
ECDH-ES + HKDF-512 on X448, which no published example covers: the 56-byte keys of RFC 7748, and HKDF over SHA-512 deriving a 192-bit content key.

ECDH-ES + HKDF-256 on X25519 delivering a 256-bit ChaCha20/Poly1305 key directly: two things EVQI Transport §7.2 names for encrypting end to end through a Local Controller — ECDH-ES + HKDF-256 to reach the one recipient, ChaCha20-Poly1305 as one of the two AEADs — here combined. COSE_KDF_Context names the content algorithm, 24, and asks for 256 bits — the place a mistake shared by both sides would hide, because a context built wrongly on both sides still opens. No published example combines ECDH-ES with ChaCha20/Poly1305, so the expected secret, context, key and message are the generator's own, computed from the noble primitives through the same hand-written CBOR that must reproduce p256-hkdf-256-01 before anything is written, with ChaCha20/Poly1305 held to RFC 8439 Section 2.8.2 first. That makes them independent of both implementations, not published by anyone.

ECDH-ES + HKDF-256 on P-256 to a recipient named by its certificate: the recipient structure carries x5t (RFC 9360, header parameter 34) — the SHA-256 COSE_CertHash of the station's renewed key-agreement certificate from tools/CertificateCorpus — and no kid, which is how EVQI Transport §6.8 addresses a recipient that holds more than one key during a renewal. The thumbprint, secret, context, key and message are computed by this generator; each implementation must also confirm that the certificate certifies the receiving key, open the other's message given that certificate, and open it without one, since a caller who names no certificate must see no change. Note what x5t is: a selector, not a protected statement. It sits in the unprotected bucket, nothing authenticates it, and a matching thumbprint proves nothing — it only says which key to use. Read as evidence of anything, it is a vulnerability.
ECDH-ES + A128KW on brainpoolP256r1, the curve of the meter certificates this project turns on, which no published example covers.

ECDH-ES + A192KW, which is the case above with exactly one thing changed: the recipient key and the ephemeral key are the same, so the agreed secret is the same, and the difference is only how many bytes HKDF is asked for and which AES width wraps the content key with them - 24 instead of 16. The middle width had no vector anywhere, here or among the published examples, although the description of this file has named it since the file existed.

ECDH-ES + HKDF-256 on X25519 with an HKDF salt and both parties named: PartyU with an identity and an integer nonce, PartyV with an identity and other information. All of it travels in the recipient's headers (-20 to -26) and all of it enters COSE_KDF_Context, so a receiver that read one field differently derives another key and opens nothing. No published example carries any of it.

Two ECDH-ES key-wrap recipients on different curves — A128KW on P-384 and A256KW on secp256k1 — each receiving the one content key through a key agreed with it alone. Only key wrap allows this; a directly agreed key belongs to one recipient. The message is opened with the first recipient's key.

ECDH-ES + HKDF-256 delivering an HMAC 384/384 key directly to a COSE_Mac on P-384. The derived key is as wide as the hash, 48 bytes — what the published examples derive for HMAC 512/512, and what RFC 9053 Section 3.1 asks an HMAC key to be.

cases.reason: the ephemeral point does not lie on P-256
cases.description: An invalid-curve attack on the static recipient key. The ephemeral point (5, 0) is not on P-256 but on a curve sharing its a and not its b, where it has order two; the recipient key is odd, so an implementation that neither checks the point nor consults b computes the point itself as the product and 5 as the secret — and this message is encrypted under the key that secret derives. It opens for exactly the implementation that skipped the check; repeated with points of other small orders, that oracle hands over the static private key. RFC 9053 §6.3.1.1 names a check without making it a MUST. Both implementations must refuse.

cases.reason: the ephemeral X25519 key is the point u = 0, whose secret is all zeroes
cases.description: An ephemeral X25519 key of u = 0. Every product with it is zero, so the secret is known to everybody — and the message is encrypted under the key that zero secret derives, so it opens for an implementation that does not check. OKP has no point validation in RFC 9053; RFC 7748 §6.1's check of the output for all zeroes is the substitute. Both implementations must refuse.

cases.reason: the ephemeral X25519 key is the point u = 1, of small order, whose secret is all zeroes
cases.description: The same with u = 1, a point of small order that is not zero: an implementation that checks its INPUT for zero lets it through, one that checks the OUTPUT as RFC 7748 §6.1 says does not. The secret is again all zeroes and the message opens for whoever did not look. Both implementations must refuse.

cases.reason: the recipient names a certificate by x5t that is not the one of the key in hand (EVQI Transport §6.8)
cases.description: A station during a renewal: it holds its old key-agreement key with the old certificate, and this recipient names the RENEWED certificate by x5t. EVQI Transport §6.8: the recipient "refuses a thumbprint that matches none of its certificates instead of trying its keys in turn" — stated, not recommended, so this is normative. The message is encrypted for the OLD key all the same, which anybody can arrange, since nothing authenticates a recipient's unprotected bucket: an implementation that ignores the thumbprint tries the old key, derives the right content key and opens it. Opening is therefore the one wrong answer, and no error text is judged. The control beside it: the same message, opened with the same key and no certificate, must open — otherwise a refusal here would prove nothing. x5t is a selector, not a protected statement.
